query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, physically vapor-deposited alumina (Al2O3) coating on cast HfNbTaTiZr will act as an effective oxygen barrier at high temperatures, significantly reducing oxygen ingress while preserving the alloy’s inherent mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr showing 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (at 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) but with poor high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Apply a ~2 μm thick Al2O3 coating via physical vapor deposition (PVD) uniformly onto the surface of the cast alloy.
generation.conditions: Expose coated samples to an oxidizing environment (laboratory air) at 1000 °C for 100 hours; subsequent mechanical testing under tensile loading at strain rates in the range of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ at similar temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous, adherent alumina layer deposited on the surface.
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 coating provides a dense, thermally stable barrier that limits oxygen diffusion into the alloy, thereby mitigating internal oxidation and preserving the underlying microstructure responsible for ductility and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the coated samples will show significantly lower oxygen uptake (evidenced by thinner oxide scales or absence of deep penetration) and retain similar yield strength and ductility after high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr under identical high-temperature exposure conditions exhibits significant oxidation leading to degraded mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to hold under the specified temperature (1000 °C), exposure time (100 hours), and mechanical-loading boundaries (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹). Exceeding these conditions (e.g., higher temperatures, longer exposures, or loading beyond the alloy’s limits) might lead to coating failure or degradation of mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the long-term adhesion stability of the PVD Al2O3 coating under thermal cycling and mechanical loading. The potential for coating spallation or cracking under realistic service conditions is not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the applied ~2 μm PVD Al2O3 coating and another uncoated (as-cast). Expose both sets to 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. After exposure, perform standardized tensile tests at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ at 1000 °C. In parallel, use surface analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS) to measure the thickness and continuity of the oxide scales on the surfaces.
measurements: Mass gain and oxide scale thickness after exposure (as a proxy for oxygen ingress).
Tensile yield strength and ductility (percent elongation) measured at high temperature.
Inspection for coating integrity (presence of cracks, spallation, or delamination) using microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples show no significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar mass gain and oxide scale thickness as the uncoated samples) or if the mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) are degraded relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
